So, in addition to defining what a strategy is,&nbsp;&nbsp; we'll also look at how to&nbsp; recognize bad strategies. &nbsp; The insights in this video are based on the&nbsp; book 'Good Strategy Bad Strategy' written&nbsp;&nbsp; by one of the world's most famous&nbsp; strategists: Richard Rumelt. &nbsp; According to Rumelt, the core of a strategy&nbsp; is always the same: identifying the critical&nbsp;&nbsp; factors of a situation and designing a way to&nbsp; coordinate and focus actions to address those&nbsp;&nbsp; factors. Therefore, a strategy is more than&nbsp; just a way to reach a goal; a good strategy&nbsp;&nbsp; recognizes the challenges ahead and finds a way&nbsp; to overcome them with a coordinated approach. &nbsp; Many people associate strategy only with&nbsp; the big-picture overall direction chosen,&nbsp;&nbsp; disconnected from specific actions.

But this&nbsp; definition is quite incomplete because it&nbsp;&nbsp; leaves a gap on how to actually implement it. Strategy has a logical structure, which Rumelt&nbsp;&nbsp; calls "The kernel," consisting&nbsp; of three elements: a diagnosis,&nbsp;&nbsp; a guiding policy, and coherent action. The initial diagnosis defines "WHY"&nbsp;&nbsp; something needs to be done, the guiding&nbsp; policy defines "WHAT" needs to be done,&nbsp;&nbsp; while the definition of coherent actions&nbsp; explains "HOW" it should be done. &nbsp; Now, before delving into the details&nbsp; of this correct definition of strategy&nbsp;&nbsp; and explaining its three components,&nbsp; let me clarify what Bad Strategy is. &nbsp; We can summarize cases of bad strategy&nbsp; into four categories, which I'm sure you've&nbsp;&nbsp; encountered. 1.

Fluff &nbsp; Here people talk in a complicated and confusing&nbsp; way to make simple things seem more important than&nbsp;&nbsp; they actually are. They often use fancy words to&nbsp; make it seem like they're talking about something&nbsp;&nbsp; smart. Here's a real example from an American bank&nbsp; that says: “Our fundamental strategy is one of&nbsp;&nbsp; customer-centric intermediation.” WHAT?!?! &nbsp; Here’s another example: “Our strategic imperative&nbsp; is to leverage our world-class capabilities and&nbsp;&nbsp; innovative mindset to deliver unparalleled value&nbsp; and transformative outcomes for our diverse global&nbsp;&nbsp; customer base.” Again WHAT?!?! &nbsp; 2.

Failure to face the challenge A bad strategy doesn't recognize or understand&nbsp;&nbsp; the problem clearly. If you don't get what the&nbsp; problem is, you can't figure out if a strategy is&nbsp;&nbsp; good or how to make it better. Without seeing and&nbsp; studying the things that are getting in your way,&nbsp;&nbsp; you don't really have a strategy. You&nbsp; might just have a big goal, a budget,&nbsp;&nbsp; or a list of things you hope will work out. For example, imagine your sales are going down.&nbsp;&nbsp; A bad strategy would be to add another sales&nbsp; channel instead of trying to figure out why&nbsp;&nbsp; the sales are dropping and fixing that.

You might&nbsp; ask, "Who would make such a mistake?" Well, lots&nbsp;&nbsp; of businesses do. Think about Blockbuster, for&nbsp; instance. When Netflix started getting traction,&nbsp;&nbsp; Blockbuster didn't really understand the&nbsp; challenge and just launched a few online&nbsp;&nbsp; services without a real analysis of the&nbsp; commitments and investments in technology&nbsp;&nbsp; required. And we all know how that ended... 3. Mistaking Strategy for Something Else &nbsp; People get really mixed up about what strategy&nbsp; means. Some think it's about having a big vision,&nbsp;&nbsp; being a good leader, planning&nbsp; things out, or setting goals.&nbsp;&nbsp; But strategy isn't any of those things.

For instance, most corporate strategic&nbsp;&nbsp; plans are merely predictions of budgets&nbsp; and market shares over 3 or 5 years. &nbsp; Or here on YouTube, I see many content creators&nbsp; promising to reveal their "exact strategy for&nbsp;&nbsp; acquiring customers," only to explain their&nbsp; tactics, step-by-step actions they take. &nbsp; 4. Bad Strategic Objectives A leader sets strategic goals to&nbsp;&nbsp; achieve something, and that's fine. However, these&nbsp; goals are ineffective when they fail to address&nbsp;&nbsp; important problems or are not feasible. For example, you may have encountered&nbsp;&nbsp; managers or other entrepreneurs who set&nbsp; unrealistic goals without defining what&nbsp;&nbsp; changes will be made to achieve them.

A company that has grown by 10% every&nbsp;&nbsp; year might set a goal to grow by 50% this year in&nbsp; terms of revenue and customer acquisition. There&nbsp;&nbsp; is nothing wrong with being ambitious,&nbsp; but how will they do it? It's unclear,&nbsp;&nbsp; and the only thing the company does is organize a&nbsp; motivation course to encourage staff to push and&nbsp;&nbsp; commit more. It’s not difficult to foresee that in&nbsp; that way they won’t obtain a result much different&nbsp;&nbsp; from what they used to do, right? Maybe at this point, various instances&nbsp;&nbsp; come to mind where you've observed&nbsp; all of this.

But the question is,&nbsp;&nbsp; "Why is there so much bad strategy out there?" The thing is, creating a good strategy requires&nbsp;&nbsp; making choices. Instead of having vague&nbsp; aspirations, you need to make a specific&nbsp;&nbsp; decision and focus on a path and have the strength&nbsp; to say no to other potential opportunities or&nbsp;&nbsp; choices. And the act of making this choice&nbsp; is difficult and painful for many leaders. &nbsp; When you channel your forces and&nbsp; resources into one direction,&nbsp;&nbsp; it often happens that you change the routines&nbsp; and habits of many people within the company,&nbsp;&nbsp; which initially may not yield immediate results&nbsp; or may even make things worse before the strategy&nbsp;&nbsp; takes effect.

That's why strategy and changes are&nbsp; usually opposed, especially in large organizations&nbsp;&nbsp; where there are many different interests. Now that we've seen what is NOT a strategy,&nbsp;&nbsp; let's delve into Rumelt's definition&nbsp; with its three basic elements: diagnosis,&nbsp;&nbsp; guiding policy, and coherent actions. The diagnosis defines or explains the&nbsp;&nbsp; nature of the challenge, explaining "WHY"&nbsp; something needs to be done. It could be a&nbsp;&nbsp; goal to achieve or a problem to solve. A good&nbsp; diagnosis confronts the overwhelming complexity&nbsp;&nbsp; of the situation you're facing and simplifies it,&nbsp; identifying the fundamental aspects to consider. &nbsp; So first, you need to understand what's happening,&nbsp; rather than immediately decide what to do.

Like&nbsp;&nbsp; a doctor who, before providing treatment to a&nbsp; patient, examines and analyzes the situation. &nbsp; For instance, you might have a business that&nbsp; relies on traffic generated from Google. Analyzing&nbsp;&nbsp; the situation, you notice that the traffic&nbsp; is decreasing. You need to understand why:&nbsp;&nbsp; has the algorithm changed and penalized the&nbsp; site? Are people using Google less because&nbsp;&nbsp; there are viable AI alternatives nowadays? Was the&nbsp; site riding a market trend that is now fading? &nbsp; You realize that based on the analyses you conduct&nbsp; and the answers you provide to questions like&nbsp;&nbsp; these, your strategy could change significantly.&nbsp; The better you become at analyzing situations,&nbsp;&nbsp; the better strategies you'll create because&nbsp; there's a subjective element to all of this. &nbsp; After conducting the analysis, you move on&nbsp; to the Guiding Policy, which is the general&nbsp;&nbsp; approach chosen to manage or overcome the&nbsp; identified obstacles and achieve the selected&nbsp;&nbsp; goal.

Essentially, it explains "WHAT" you do. For example, Wells Fargo's guiding policy,&nbsp;&nbsp; which they call strategy, is to leverage&nbsp; their network's effect to cross-sell various&nbsp;&nbsp; financial products to customers. The more&nbsp; products they sell, the more they can get&nbsp;&nbsp; to know the customers and serve them better. Many, like Wells Fargo, call the guiding policy&nbsp;&nbsp; ‘strategy’, but it's not the same thing.&nbsp; The guiding policy is just one of the&nbsp;&nbsp; three elements necessary for a good strategy. Or in the previous example of website traffic,&nbsp;&nbsp; after establishing that the problem&nbsp; relates to your outdated content,&nbsp;&nbsp; you could set a guiding policy aimed at&nbsp; identifying a new trend relevant to your site&nbsp;&nbsp; to capitalize on and create new content about.

So, once you've determined "WHAT" to do,&nbsp;&nbsp; it's time to move on to the "HOW," defining the&nbsp; coherent actions. This isn't about getting into&nbsp;&nbsp; the nitty-gritty details. It's about establishing&nbsp; the set of actions that will be taken to implement&nbsp;&nbsp; the guiding policy established. These steps must&nbsp; be coordinated and consistent with each other. &nbsp; What you don't want is to have&nbsp; various disconnected actions or&nbsp;&nbsp; projects that create dispersion and&nbsp; often conflict with each other. &nbsp; For instance, regarding the earlier website&nbsp; example, a set of disjointed and incorrect actions&nbsp;&nbsp; would be to hire a new writer to work on Content&nbsp; B, redesign the website and graphics, rebrand the&nbsp;&nbsp; business, and launch a Facebook Ads campaign.

Instead, a set of coordinated and correct actions&nbsp;&nbsp; would be: research the new market trends&nbsp; relevant to your industry, identify the new&nbsp;&nbsp; trend to capitalize on that fits your audience.&nbsp; While continuing to create content about the&nbsp;&nbsp; old trend that your readers are loyal to, begin&nbsp; creating content for the newly identified trend.&nbsp;&nbsp; Gradually increase the new content and decrease&nbsp; the old content while monitoring the results,&nbsp;&nbsp; until a complete transition is complete. At this stage, I'd like to point out two things. &nbsp; Firstly, many details are missing in the set of&nbsp; actions described, such as how to do them, when to&nbsp;&nbsp; do them, in what order, by when, etc.

These will&nbsp; be addressed during the planning phase, which is&nbsp;&nbsp; a subsequent step but not part of the strategy. Secondly, the kernel does not include the vision,&nbsp;&nbsp; hierarchies of goals and objectives, references&nbsp; to time span, etc. These are important but&nbsp;&nbsp; accessory elements to the strategy. Now, armed with this information,&nbsp;&nbsp; you can evaluate the effectiveness of strategies&nbsp; you come across, immediately identifying whether&nbsp;&nbsp; they are full of fluff or have real substance.&nbsp; But most importantly, you can use this three-step&nbsp;&nbsp; approach to create your own business strategies.

In my opinion, this already brings a lot of&nbsp;&nbsp; clarity and removes confusion, but this is just&nbsp; the beginning. Yes, because in the next video,&nbsp;&nbsp; I'll explain the levers to use to refine your&nbsp; strategic skills. You'll find the video here&nbsp;&nbsp; as soon as it's ready. In the meantime, if you&nbsp; haven't already, subscribe to the channel to be&nbsp;&nbsp; notified as soon as it's published. To the Founders’ Success.
